contract.intent: THE WORKER HAS ONE DOOR, AND IT ONLY OPENS ON A NEW SUBMISSION. `submit!` runs the exit gate's review worker as the door to the gate (12/22), and NOTHING ELSE CAN: `submit!` refuses a re-submission by name (`already-submitted`), the frame returns `blocked-at-gate` at an undecided submission BEFORE it reaches `reviewGate` (frame.ts:318 returns ahead of the call at frame.ts:369), and no route builds a review at all. MEASURED CONSEQUENCE, TODAY — EIGHT confirm gates stand undecided: 12/10, 12/11, 12/12, 12/13, 12/14, 12/21, 12/22 and 12/23. Every one was opened BEFORE the worker existed in the running binary, and `ann brief` says the same sentence for every one of them: NO REVIEW HAS LANDED. So the premise D-1 rests on — the human LEAVES the exit gate — holds only for gates opened after the worker shipped, and every gate already standing is the human's by accident of TIMING rather than by design. That is the burden leg 12 exists to remove, still owed on eight cards. THIS NODE ADDS THE MISSING GESTURE: `ann gate! <id> confirm --review` runs the SAME worker against the submission ALREADY STANDING, and its verdict lands through the SAME writer. It is a second CALLER of `runGateReview`, never a second path — no new write, no new event type, no new state, no new loop, and the model is still never asked for a verdict. WHAT IS EXPLICITLY OUT OF SCOPE: every route and the served card (the flag is CLI-only and UNREACHABLE from `POST /api/gate` by construction — that route dispatches the CLI's own argv, but its body has no field that can carry the flag, and that absence is PINNED so a later hand cannot widen it silently); the GRILL, which stays the human's (12/22's premise, untouched — and the operator restated it: the flag is the END GATE's and nothing else); a DECIDED gate (the flag requires an undecided submission and refuses otherwise — a decided gate is a decided gate, and re-deciding one is not this node's to invent); the close FLOOR, which is not re-read (it is the SUBMISSION's predicate, enforced once when the gate opened — a floor that has since lapsed shows up where it always does, at the close, and this flag must not become a second place that rule lives); and THE VERDICTS THEMSELVES, which are the worker's to reach and not this node's to arrange — the operator's own instruction is 'we will see how it works for now', so the demonstration RUNS and RECORDS rather than aiming at an outcome.
acceptanceCriteria: AC-1 — THE GESTURE, AND THE FOUR THINGS IT REFUSES. `ann gate! <id> confirm --review` runs the exit gate's worker against `<id>`'s undecided confirm submission. FOUR named refusals, each decided BEFORE anything is spent — so a refused gesture costs no model call — and each with ZERO writes: `review-not-confirm` (a grill: the entry gate stays the human's) · `review-takes-no-decision` (an `accept`/`reject` positional given beside the flag: the flag IS the decision request, so giving both is two gestures in one command) · `review-no-submission` (no undecided submission standing — the gate is already decided, or was never opened) · `review-with-flag` (`--force` or `--transfer`/`--scope` composed with it). Pinned by test at every edge, including that each refusal leaves the event list byte-identical.

AC-2 — ONE WORKER, ONE WRITER, ONE PATH. The flag calls `runGateReview` — the same function `submit!` and the frame call, with no wrapper and no second implementation — and its `accept`/`rework` lands through `commands.gate` with the worker's ENGINE-STAMPED actor, exactly as at a fresh submission. Pinned by test: the flag introduces no event type, no state and no write path; and the review material and the derived verdict are identical whether the review was reached by `submit!` or by the flag (same bytes, same rule, one derivation).

AC-3 — THREE ANSWERS THAT STAND, AND ONE THAT FAILS. `accept` and `rework` are reported with the findings count and the why/feedback the worker recorded, exactly as the frame reports them. `human` — an open concern with no defect, or the reject bound where the worker is OUT — is reported as a truthful OUTCOME, exit 0, NAMING the reason: nothing written, the submission standing, no rejection burned, the card unchanged. An ABSENCE (no provider, an unreachable endpoint, an unparseable reply) is different in KIND and is a NAMED FAILURE with zero writes: the operator asked for a review and did not get one, and AC-6's rule (absence degrades to the human, visibly) governs a submission NOBODY ASKED to review — reusing it here would swallow a request by dressing it as a degradation. The operator settled this reading explicitly: FAIL. Pinned by test at each of the four.

AC-4 — UNREACHABLE FROM EVERY ROUTE, BY CONSTRUCTION. `POST /api/gate` dispatches the CLI's own argv built from `{id, gate, decision, feedback}`; it has no field that can carry the flag, so the gesture is CLI-only by construction rather than by convention. Pinned by test: a body carrying an extra `review` field decides nothing differently (the dispatched argv is unchanged), and the route's own shape is asserted — so a later hand adding the field has to delete a test, not merely forget one.

AC-5 — THE DEMONSTRATION, ON THE GATES THAT MOTIVATED IT. The flag is run against the live undecided confirm gates, and EVERY VERDICT IS RECORDED AS IT LANDS: which the worker accepted, which it routed to rework, and which it left to the human with its reason. The AC is the RECORD, not the outcome — a `rework` on a delivery days old is not pre-judged and is not a failure of this node; it is the engine working, and the operator's instruction is to run it and see. The bound case is included: at a gate whose rejections are exhausted the flag reports the human card WITHOUT spending a model call, and the record says so.

AC-6 — THE SPEC CARRIES IT. `docs/gate-cadence.md` §7 states the gesture and the hole it fills: the worker's door is the SUBMISSION, so a gate standing open when the worker was absent — or before it existed — had no door at all until this flag. The section names the four refusals and says plainly that the flag is CLI-only and route-unreachable. The document's claim and the code's behaviour are the same claim, not two.

AC-7 — NO REGRESSION. `npm test` green, `npm run typecheck` and `npm run build` clean, the captured checks recorded via `capture!`, `ann check` + `ann verify` clean on the live journey, committed with structured evidence (F-AC18).
expectedOutputs: the --review flag on gate!: parsed and guarded in the CLI handler beside --force, with the four named refusals and zero writes on each (src/surface)
the flag's three answers and its one failure, reported to the operator with the worker's own words (src/surface)
tests: every refusal edge, the identical-material/identical-verdict claim, the four outcomes, and the route-unreachability pin (src/surface, src/flow)
the recorded demonstration against live undecided confirm gates, with every verdict as it landed (the journey record)
docs/gate-cadence.md §7: the gesture, the hole it fills, the four refusals, and the CLI-only boundary (docs)

openQuestions.question: Which gates does the operator run the flag against, and is a worker `rework` on a days-old delivery an answer to accept? The eight were submitted 2026-09-25/26 and the material assembly has changed since (12/23's delivery), so a re-review judges old bytes with today's reviewer — which is the point — but a `rework` verdict sends a finished delivery back to an executor days after it landed.
openQuestions.defaultIfUnanswered: Run it against the live undecided confirm gates and RECORD EVERY VERDICT as it lands, without pre-judging them — a `rework` is the engine working, and the delivery that comes back is a second round with its own evidence, exactly as a human's rejection is. The narrower alternative (review nothing until the operator names each gate) leaves the backlog this node exists for untouched.

openQuestions.question: An ABSENCE at `--review` — a NAMED FAILURE (this node's AC-3), or the same visible degradation a submission gets? AC-3 reads the two as different in kind: at a submission nobody asked to review, degrading visibly is right; at an explicit `--review` the operator asked and did not get one, so a silent degradation would be the swallow AC-6 exists to prevent. The alternative is one rule for the provider being down on every path.
openQuestions.defaultIfUnanswered: FAIL — named, non-zero, zero writes, per AC-3.
